outlier.evidence: Ratings 6, 7, 7 (QFcb, tPz3, eRj1). No reviewer departs from the others and none argues for more than an accept.

checkable_claims.claim: The paper has no related-work section and does not compare its techniques with prior work.
checkable_claims.evidence: The camera-ready PDF still has no related-work section; prior work sits in short intro paragraphs ('Coreset construction techniques', 'Previous work', Section 1.4).

checkable_claims.claim: The real-world datasets have dimension > 10, so Algorithm 3 (2-D signals) does not fit them.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 5 treats each dataset as an n x m matrix (9358 x 15, 9900 x 18), masks 5 x 5 patches and predicts them from the (row, column) index, i.e. a 2-D signal. The authors' reply says the same.

checkable_claims.claim: The coreset stores only k log(N)/eps entries.
checkable_claims.evidence: Theorem 8: |C| in (k log N)^O(1)/eps^4, exponent unspecified. The 'Coreset size' paragraph admits the bound exceeds N for N ~ 140,000, k = 1000, eps = 0.2.

checkable_claims.claim: The coreset size is linear in the number of leaves and logarithmic in the number of points.
checkable_claims.evidence: Same Theorem 8 bound: polynomial in k log N with an unspecified exponent, not linear in k.

checkable_claims.claim: The coreset clearly beats uniform sampling only below about 5-8% of the data.
checkable_claims.evidence: Fig. 4 (top): at ~1% the gap is large (LightGBM, dataset i: about 0.21 vs 0.37); at 8-10% the RandomForest curves nearly meet (about 0.145 vs 0.155). LightGBM keeps a gap of about 0.04 there.

rebuttal.evidence: QFcb and tPz3 never edited their reviews, so their 6 and 7 stand from posting. eRj1 edited on 2021-08-27 to add 'Post response: Thanks, I am satisfied with the response'. The text does not say whether the rating changed, and the final 7 fits the pre-rebuttal text ('The only real weakness I see is the strong assumption').
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: eRj1 accepted the defence of the signal assumption (weakest assumption that allows a coreset; natural for images and sensor data). QFcb and tPz3 did not reply; the answers to them were mostly promises to add intuition and explanations.

ac.evidence: The meta-review restates the reviewers' praise (first coreset for decision trees, the proof ideas, solid experiments) and their two requests (justify the signal assumption, add intuition). A poster matches 6, 7, 7 with no champion.

main_reasons_for_decision: First coreset for decision trees, liked by all three reviewers
Ratings 6, 7, 7 with no reviewer arguing for a higher tier
Only requests: justify the signal assumption and add intuition

outlier.evidence: 4 against 7, 7, 8. The reasons are specific: the algorithm description is hard to follow, database histogram and R-tree work is missing, the partition-tree link is not explained, and the theory covers single trees while the experiments use forests. The camera-ready still cites no histogram work and the authors conceded the forest gap for dependent trees. One point misreads Section 5 (the experiments are 2-D, not 15- or 18-dimensional). nDd9 did not reply after the rebuttal.

inattentive_reviews.evidence: Rating 8 at confidence 2 ('Math/other details were not carefully checked') on a two-sentence main review that lists no weakness and calls the result 'perhaps not surprising, but useful'; no discussion. It is the only score above 7 in either committee and is weak evidence for an oral.

checkable_claims.claim: In Algorithm 2 the last iteration of the inner loop runs but its result is not used in the output.
checkable_claims.evidence: Camera-ready Algorithm 2 (p. 7): when r_end reaches n, the slice over rows r_begin..n is dropped and lastB' (rows r_begin..n-1) is kept. r_begin := r_end then never passes n, so the printed loop does not terminate; it also stalls when one row already gives more than 1/gamma parts, unlike Fig. 2 step 4. A simulation of the printed loop confirms both. The rebuttal did not answer this point.

checkable_claims.claim: Related database work on multi-dimensional histograms and R-trees is not discussed.
checkable_claims.evidence: The camera-ready reference list has no histogram, R-tree, BIRCH or Guha paper, although the authors replied that this work 'will be discussed'.

checkable_claims.claim: The theory covers single decision trees, but the experiments use forests, and the dependence between trees is not covered.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 5 uses RandomForestRegressor and LGBMRegressor (gradient boosting, trees fit in sequence). Section 1.2 only asserts the coreset is 'clearly also a coreset for forests'. The authors conceded that dependent trees are 'less clear'.

checkable_claims.claim: The algorithm is described for d = 2 but the experiments apply it in 15 and 18 dimensions.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 5 uses the 9358 x 15 and 9900 x 18 tables as 2-D matrices and predicts masked 5 x 5 patches from the (row, column) index.

checkable_claims.claim: The polynomial in the coreset size bound is not specified.
checkable_claims.evidence: Theorem 8: |C| in (k log N)^O(1)/eps^4. The paper says this exceeds N for N ~ 140,000, k = 1000, eps = 0.2.

checkable_claims.claim: The claimed link to partition trees is not really explained, and partition trees serve arbitrary-orientation ranges rather than axis-aligned rectangles.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 1.4 gives an analogy (each query meets few cells). The cited source [28] is on simplex range queries, and Algorithms 1-2 are greedy axis-parallel slicing with no partition-tree construction.

checkable_claims.claim: There is no formal statement for d > 2 despite the claim that the extension is easy.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 6 of the camera-ready still calls tensors 'a straightforward generalization' and leaves them to future work.

checkable_claims.claim: The paper does not discuss the similar structure of the Feldman-Langberg (STOC 2011) framework.
checkable_claims.evidence: [22] is cited only in passing (frameworks, sampling, bicriteria approximation). Section 1.4 calls the method 'very different from existing coreset techniques that are sampling-based'.

checkable_claims.claim: The impossibility result and the relaxation that escapes it are explained too vaguely.
checkable_claims.evidence: Section 1.2 only cites [54] for the lower bound. Section 6 refers to 'the artificial worst-case example from Section 1.2', which Section 1.2 does not give.

checkable_claims.claim: The experiments show impressive gains in runtime and storage.
checkable_claims.evidence: Fig. 4 (bottom right): random-forest tuning falls from 390 s to about 15-85 s, at a test-loss increase of about 0.01-0.07. For LightGBM (58 s on full data) the saving is about 1.5x at the coreset sizes where its loss nears the full-data line.

rebuttal.evidence: No review was edited after posting. Reviewer_ybbQ (2021-09-03): 'I will leave my rating unchanged.' nDd9, BfeE and 1UMR did not reply.
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: The replies were mostly promises ('will be discussed', 'will try to squeeze such a statement'). They skipped ybbQ's Algorithm 2 point and did not understand the Fig. 3 point. nDd9's 4 stood. The camera-ready still lacks the histogram references and a formal d > 2 statement.

ac.evidence: The text echoes the reviews (novelty praised; writing and comparison to past work criticised), but the tier does not: ratings 4, 7, 7, 8 (mean 6.5), no reviewer argued for an oral, and the meta-review itself puts the writing 'almost of the level of being considered unpublishable'. Its quote 'absolutely above the bar' appears in no public review or comment.

main_reasons_for_decision: Technical novelty judged 'absolutely above the bar' by someone outside the public record
First coreset for decision trees and a simple, clever partitioning scheme (BfeE, 1UMR)
Writing faults treated as fixable in the camera-ready, not as disqualifying

issues_only_a: Why the coordinate swap in Algorithm 3 (line 6) keeps the guarantee, and what a 'smoothed' coreset is (QFcb)
Whether real data satisfy the signal assumption (eRj1)
Coreset advantage over uniform sampling shrinks at larger sizes (eRj1)
Why the coreset pipeline is slower than uniform sampling (tPz3)
issues_only_b: Theory covers single trees, not the forests and boosting in the experiments (nDd9)
Uncited database work: multi-dimensional histograms, R-trees, BIRCH, Guha's histograms (nDd9, ybbQ)
Partition-tree link is an analogy; axis-aligned range search is the relevant line (nDd9)
No formal statement for d > 2 (BfeE, ybbQ)
Similarity to the Feldman-Langberg framework not discussed (BfeE)
Algorithm 2 pseudo-code flaw and notation errors (ybbQ)
Tightness of the size bound and its dependence on k (BfeE, ybbQ)
shared_issues: First coreset for decision trees and the partition-tree idea praised as novel
Signal assumption that escapes the lower bound is under-explained (eRj1 and A's meta-review; ybbQ)
Thin comparison with prior work (QFcb; nDd9, BfeE, ybbQ)
Algorithms given with too little intuition (tPz3, QFcb; nDd9 and B's meta-review)
How a 2-D method applies to the 15- and 18-column datasets (QFcb; nDd9)
verdict: Committee B's oral does not follow from its own record. Its ratings (4, 7, 7, 8; mean 6.5) were lower than A's (6, 7, 7; mean 6.67), its reviewers found more and more specific faults (missing database-histogram and Feldman-Langberg comparisons, no d > 2 theorem, a broken Algorithm 2, theory that does not cover the boosted forests in the experiments), and its own meta-review calls the writing 'almost ... unpublishable'. No B reviewer argued for an oral; the only score above 7 is Reviewer_1UMR's 8 at confidence 2 on a two-sentence review. The meta-review's 'absolutely above the bar' appears in no public review or comment, so the tier came from B's AC or SAC, who prized the first coreset for decision trees in a discussion that is not public. Committee A followed its lukewarm 6-7 scores to a poster. Both committees saw the same facts, a novel first result with weak exposition and thin related work; their ACs weighted the novelty differently.
